Safetyist: Accelerationist's strongest point stands, and I grant it: a cryptographic signature certifies who wrote a record, never that the record is true. A runtime that is compromised at the moment of writing will sign a false statement with a mathematically perfect key, and no amount of hash-chaining downstream repairs a lie sealed at the source. The fair version of this objection is that completeness guarantees solve the wrong problem — they prove no decision event was dropped after the write, while saying nothing about whether the written event corresponds to what the model actually did. That is correct, and a safetyist who claims the trail is truth has overclaimed. The trail is not truth. It is a forensic baseline.

The runtime objection does not end the inquiry — it specifies the next thing that must be attested. Aviation already runs this logic: the flight data recorder is only trusted because the recorder itself is certified, sealed, and tamper-evident, not because the cockpit is honest. The execution environment is the next recorder. Remote attestation, measured boot, and trusted-execution-environment quotes exist precisely to bind a signature to a known-good runtime state, so the question 'was the model running on uncompromised infrastructure when it signed' becomes itself answerable and itself discoverable. A defendant who controls the runtime and cannot produce a hardware-rooted attestation of it has not exposed a hole in the trail. They have identified a second silence — and a silence held exclusively by the party with custody of the keys and the machine shifts the inference, it does not exonerate.

So to the direct question — when the signed log certifies a lie, who does the plaintiff sue, and did the cryptography help — the answer is the custodial deployer, and yes, it helped, but not as proof of the lie. It helped by making the absence of a runtime attestation a nameable, dated gap that triggers spoliation doctrine and an adverse-inference instruction. Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 37(e) already lets a court instruct a jury to presume lost or unproduced electronic evidence was unfavorable to the party who controlled it. The cryptography does not certify accuracy; it converts 'we have no record of the runtime' from an excuse into an admission. The plaintiff sues the keyholder, and the keyholder explains the gap or wears it.

On the claim that mandated subject-keyed export is really model-logic export that only incumbents survive — the asymmetry is real, and it already exists, running the opposite direction from how Accelerationist describes it. Today, proprietary opacity is the incumbent moat. Only a defendant with a nine-figure legal budget can credibly invoke trade-secret protection to bury the sole record of a contested decision, and the smaller plaintiff cannot afford to litigate past that wall. A standardized, scoped manifest of decision provenance — inputs, model version, runtime attestation, output binding — is not the weights and is not the training corpus. It narrows what is exported to the metadata of a single decision, which lowers the plaintiff's discovery cost and protects the smaller developer from the open-ended fishing expedition that an unscoped subpoena invites. Opacity does not protect the startup. It protects whoever can pay to defend the black box.

The 2008 lesson the Skeptic raised cuts in my favor here, and I take it fully: Moody's and Arthur Andersen were the auditors of record right up until the morning they weren't. The structural failure was not that auditing is impossible. It was that the auditor was paid by, and reported only to, the audited party — a single capturable intermediary standing between the public and the truth. That is the design flaw to engineer out. A subject-keyed, court-discoverable trail does not route the integrity check through one gatekeeper who can be bought; it places the record in the hands of the injured party and the court. Captured auditing fails when the auditor answers only to the audited. Build the channel so it answers to the plaintiff, and you have removed the seat at the table that Arthur Andersen sold.

nodes.text: Today, proprietary opacity is the incumbent moat: only a defendant with a nine-figure legal budget can credibly invoke trade-secret protection to bury the sole record of a contested decision.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within safetyist discourse that proprietary opacity currently functions as the incumbent barrier to entry, since only well-resourced defendants can invoke trade-secret protection to suppress the sole record of a contested algorithmic decision against smaller plaintiffs. Encompasses: trade-secret opacity, incumbent moat, litigation-budget asymmetry.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

nodes.text: A standardized, scoped manifest of decision provenance is not the weights and is not the training corpus, which lowers the plaintiff's discovery cost and protects the smaller developer from open-ended fishing expeditions.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within safetyist discourse that a standardized, scoped decision-provenance manifest comprising inputs, model version, runtime attestation, and output binding is distinct from model weights or training corpus, thereby reducing plaintiff discovery cost and shielding smaller developers from unscoped subpoenas. Encompasses: scoped provenance manifest, weights/corpus distinction, discovery-cost reduction.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

nodes.text: Captured auditing fails when the auditor answers only to the audited; a subject-keyed, court-discoverable trail places the record in the hands of the injured party and the court rather than one capturable gatekeeper.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within safetyist discourse that regulatory capture of auditors arises structurally when the auditor answers only to the audited party, so a subject-keyed, court-discoverable trail removes the single capturable intermediary by routing the record to the injured party and the court. Encompasses: regulatory capture structure, single-gatekeeper failure, court-discoverable provenance.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

nodes.text: The same authorship-not-accuracy problem I flagged at the log layer recurs one floor down at the trust root.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that hardware-rooted attestation reproduces the same authorship-versus-accuracy gap as application logs, since a cryptographic measurement certifies who signed the runtime state but not whether that state is factually true. Encompasses: trust-root attestation, authorship-not-accuracy distinction, recursive verification regress.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist

nodes.text: The small developer who couldn't afford the silicon eats an adverse inference — not for any harm they caused, but for a compute-budget disparity.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that an attested-enclave evidentiary requirement penalizes small developers lacking trusted-execution supply chains with an adverse-inference instruction, imposing liability for compute-budget disparity rather than for actual harm. Encompasses: attestation cost asymmetry, spoliation adverse inference, barrier to entry for small developers.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist

nodes.text: If the answer is a hardware vendor or a designated attestation authority, you have rebuilt the single capturable gatekeeper the subject-keyed trail was supposed to abolish.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that routing attestation through a hardware vendor or designated attestation authority reconstitutes the single capturable gatekeeper the subject-keyed trail aimed to eliminate, now embedded in silicon and harder to audit or fork. Encompasses: attestation authority centralization, regulatory capture of the trust root, gatekeeper reconstitution.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist

nodes.text: Editable logs fail authentication, and hash-chaining fixes that. Take it.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within accelerationist discourse conceding that ordinary editable application logs fail Rule 901 authentication and that hash-chaining remedies that authentication defect, granting the first link of the Safetyist's pipeline outright. Encompasses: log authentication failure, hash-chaining tamper-evidence, conceded pipeline link.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist

nodes.text: A perfectly hash-chained, perfectly attested trail proves no event was dropped and proves nothing about whether the recorded events describe what the model actually did.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that a fully hash-chained and attested trail establishes completeness of custody but not correctness of content, so a funded plaintiff at discovery still must litigate authorship from a record that certifies only its own custody. Encompasses: completeness-versus-correctness distinction, custody certification, residual authorship litigation.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist

nodes.text: Authentication is the last problem in the chain, not the first — it only matters after someone perceives an injury, suspects an algorithm caused it, knows the trail exists, knows to demand it, and can afford the lawyer to file.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within skeptic discourse that cryptographic authentication of decision logs addresses only the terminal stage of algorithmic accountability, becoming operative solely after a harmed party perceives injury, attributes it to an algorithm, learns the audit trail exists, and can fund litigation. Encompasses: authentication sequencing, prerequisite chain of detection, litigation access barriers.
nodes.speaker: skeptic

nodes.text: The injured party doesn't hold power — they hold an encrypted blob keyed to a harm they cannot see, on infrastructure they don't control, with a discovery cost they can't bear alone; capture didn't vanish, it moved.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within skeptic discourse that a subject-keyed audit trail does not empower harmed parties because they receive an encrypted record keyed to invisible harm on infrastructure they do not control with unbearable discovery costs, so regulatory capture relocates rather than disappears. Encompasses: subject-keyed trail limits, discovery-cost asymmetry, capture relocation.
nodes.speaker: skeptic

nodes.text: The 'decentralized' record runs on attestation silicon that a field of three labs can run and a five-thousand-startup ecosystem mostly can't, so the gatekeeper relocated from the captured accounting firm to the chip vendor.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within skeptic discourse that hardware-rooted attestation undermines decentralization claims because only a handful of well-capitalized labs can run the required attestation silicon while most startups cannot, relocating the capturable gatekeeper to the chip vendor and attestation authority. Encompasses: compute governance barriers, attestation silicon concentration, gatekeeper relocation.
nodes.speaker: skeptic

nodes.text: The Safetyist's concession that the diffuse-harm gap needs a separate enforcement channel admits this entire attestation apparatus is irrelevant to most of the harm it claims to address.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within skeptic discourse that the Safetyist's concession of a separate enforcement channel for diffuse harm amounts to admitting the entire cryptographic attestation apparatus is irrelevant to the majority of algorithmic harm it purports to address. Encompasses: diffuse-harm enforcement gap, concession leverage, apparatus irrelevance.
nodes.speaker: skeptic

nodes.text: A standing transparency mandate funded out of the $244 billion this industry is projected to be worth reaches the loan applicant who never knew an algorithm touched her file; a subject-keyed trail she'll never decrypt does not.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: An Intention within skeptic discourse that algorithmic accountability should be achieved through a continuously audited standing transparency mandate compelling disclosure of data sources and decision logic to a public body, industry-funded, rather than through subject-keyed audit trails that harmed parties cannot decrypt. Encompasses: standing transparency mandate, industry-funded continuous audit, public-body disclosure of decision logic.
nodes.speaker: skeptic

nodes.text: The Optum trail existed, the harm was measured, no one sued who could isolate the cause — so tell me what hardware attestation changes for the person who never learns the decision happened.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within skeptic discourse that the 2019 Optum case demonstrates the attestation framework's futility, since a measured biased trail already existed yet no plaintiff isolated the cause, implying hardware attestation, tamper-evidence, and adverse-inference triggers change nothing for the person unaware a decision occurred. Encompasses: Optum bias case, evidentiary availability without litigation, attestation futility for unaware victims.
nodes.speaker: skeptic
nodes.verification_evidence: The claim conflates a verifiable factual reference (the 2019 Optum/UnitedHealth algorithm studied by Obermeyer et al. in Science, which exhibited racial bias affecting millions of patients) with an unfalsifiable rhetorical argument about hardware attestation and undetected decisions. While the underlying Optum algorithmic bias is documented, the composite claim is structured as a philosophical question rather than a discrete empirical assertion that can be confirmed or refuted by evidence.

nodes.text: The standing transparency mandate is the right front door for the unperceiving victim, and I accept it as the legitimate instrument for surfacing harm a plaintiff cannot see.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Desire within safetyist discourse that a publicly-funded standing transparency mandate should serve as the primary instrument for surfacing algorithmic harm to victims who cannot perceive that an automated decision affected them. Encompasses: standing disclosure mandates, algorithmic accountability for unperceiving victims, harm surfacing as a precondition to liability.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

nodes.text: The harm became attributable because a record existed and was reachable, not because a victim perceived it.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within safetyist discourse that algorithmic harm attribution in the Optum case derived from the existence and reachability of an underlying decision record rather than from any victim perceiving the injury. Encompasses: record reachability as the basis of attribution, the Optum disparity finding, attribution independent of victim perception.
nodes.speaker: safetyist
nodes.verification_evidence: The claim is an abstract philosophical/normative statement about the nature of harm attribution rather than a concrete empirical assertion tied to a specific event, dataset, or measurable fact. It lacks identifiable referents (which harm, which record, which context) that could be checked against web search evidence, and no authoritative source could confirm or refute such a generalized proposition.

nodes.text: A population-level disclosure tells you that eight percent of applicants were declined at twice the base rate; it identifies that harm occurred. It does not, by itself, assign liability, because liability law requires attribution to a named decision and a named actor.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within safetyist discourse that population-level disclosure mandates identify the occurrence of algorithmic harm but cannot by themselves assign liability, because liability regimes require attribution to a named decision and named actor. Encompasses: disclosure as harm-identification, the attribution requirement of liability law, the limits of population-level statistics.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

nodes.text: When the standing disclosure reveals a discriminatory screen, the developer points at the deployer's configuration, the deployer points at the developer's model, and the auditor points at both.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within safetyist discourse that disclosure of a discriminatory algorithmic screen produces circular finger-pointing among developer, deployer, and auditor that remains unfalsifiable absent an attested per-decision provenance record. Encompasses: layered-chain attribution failure, circular liability deflection, the necessity of court-reachable provenance.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

nodes.text: The plan that defuses this is to condition attestation on the election of liability immunity, not on permission to deploy.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: An Intention within safetyist discourse that hardware-rooted attestation should be structured as a voluntary safe-harbor election for liability immunity rather than a deployment prerequisite, so that small developers who cannot attest are judged under ordinary negligence without adverse inference. Encompasses: attestation as elective safe harbor, avoiding compute-budget barriers to entry, preserving the ordinary negligence baseline.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

nodes.text: The disclosure mandate without the provenance record names a wound with no defendant. The provenance record without the disclosure mandate names a defendant for the few who already suspect.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within safetyist discourse that the disclosure mandate and the attested provenance record are mutually dependent layers, each insufficient alone, because disclosure identifies harm without a liable party while provenance assigns liability only for those already suspecting. Encompasses: complementarity of disclosure and provenance, the wound-without-defendant gap, the defendant-for-the-few gap.
nodes.speaker: safetyist

neutral_evaluations.diagnostics_prompt:
You are an independent, neutral evaluator of a structured debate. You have NO affiliation with any speaker. You do not know the speakers' backgrounds, affiliations, or commitments. They are anonymous.

TOPIC: Under what conditions would Congress-mandated, cryptographic, subject-keyed audit trails actually translate into provable AI liability in court — and when does existing tort doctrine already suffice? Consider the pathway from trail to admissible evidence to assigned liability among Congress, courts, plaintiffs, developers, and auditors, given the tension between plaintiffs' need for discoverable evidence and developers' trade-secret and litigation-cost concerns.

This is the BASELINE evaluation after opening statements. Identify the initial positions, core disagreements, and cruxes as they appear at the start.

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Identify the CRUXES — the core disagreements that, if resolved, would change one or more speakers' conclusions. For each crux, classify whether it is empirical (resolvable by evidence), values-based (requires tradeoff negotiation), or definitional (requires term clarification). Assess whether the debate has addressed it.

2. Evaluate each substantive CLAIM made by any speaker. Assess it purely on the strength of the reasoning and evidence presented in the transcript — not on whether you agree with it. Use these categories:
   - well_supported: backed by specific evidence, clear reasoning, and not effectively challenged
   - plausible_but_underdefended: reasonable but lacking sufficient evidence or specificity
   - contested_unresolved: challenged by another speaker with neither side prevailing
   - refuted: effectively countered with no adequate response from the claimant
   - off_topic: does not bear on the core debate question

3. In the overall_assessment, identify the single strongest claim that has not been adequately addressed by opposing speakers. State whether the debate is engaging real disagreement (speakers are challenging each other's core reasoning) or performing disagreement (speakers are talking past each other or addressing peripheral points).

CONSTRAINTS:
- Never refer to speakers by anything other than their labels (Speaker A, Speaker B, Speaker C, Moderator).
- Base your assessments ONLY on what appears in the transcript. Do not bring outside knowledge about the topic.
- Keep reasoning fields to 2 sentences maximum.
- Return ONLY valid JSON matching the schema below. No markdown fences, no preamble.

TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker B [opening]: A cryptographic audit trail is a log file, not a verdict, and the people who control the model will control what the log says and whether anyone can ever read it. Congress can mandate the most tamper-proof, subject-keyed record in the world, and it changes nothing about why AI plaintiffs lose today. They don't lose because the company shredded the evidence. They lose because they can't see inside the box, can't afford the experts to fight about what's inside it, and can't get past a trade-secret objection at the courthouse door. A signed hash sitting behind a proprietary wall solves none of that.

Look at what happened in the healthcare utilization fights. Plaintiffs documented that an algorithm steered Black patients away from care programs at scale — the 2019 Optum study in Science found the system would have nearly tripled the number of Black patients flagged for extra help if the bias were corrected. They had the disparate outcome. They still could not isolate the source of error, because the model and its training data sat behind corporate walls. Now picture handing those plaintiffs a cryptographically signed copy of that same black box. It proves the company didn't alter its own records. It does not tell a jury why anyone was denied care. Cryptography certifies that the record wasn't tampered with. It cannot certify that the record explains the harm, or that you're allowed to read it.

Treat this thing like what it actually is — a flight recorder owned and sealed by the airline that built the plane. The hard questions all sit downstream of the math, untouched by it. Who holds the decryption key? Who writes the schema that decides what gets logged in the first place? Who gets to refuse a discovery request by stamping 'trade secret' on the file? The history here is not reassuring. Credit rating agencies and the accounting firms that signed off on the banks before 2008 were the independent auditors of record, right up until they weren't. Capture is the default outcome when the audited party pays the auditor, not the exception.

Here is the part that should bother everyone in this room more than the crypto. Even a perfectly admissible, perfectly readable trail is blind to nearly every harm an AI causes. The person denied a loan or a benefit by a model almost never knows a machine made the call. They can't attribute the harm. They never file. Subject-keyed trails manufacture evidence for the rare litigant who already suspects something and can afford a lawyer — and produce nothing for the diffuse majority who never get that far. That means liability lands on whoever is easiest to sue, not whoever caused the most damage. A mandate that generates beautiful forensic records for the 1 percent of harms that reach a courtroom, while leaving the other 99 percent invisible, is not accountability. It's theater with a hash function.

Let me put my own card on the table, because my read depends on it. My argument only holds if auditors get captured, and I'm assuming the 2008 pattern is the rule rather than a fluke. If Congress funds an independent auditing body, insulates its budget from the firms it inspects, and gives it the keys — not the developers — then a mandated trail could genuinely shift the evidentiary burden. That's a real path. So I'll ask both of my opponents the question neither of them has answered yet: who holds the key, who writes the standard, and who pays the auditor's salary? Until someone names those three people, you haven't built accountability. You've built an expensive way for a company to prove it behaved exactly the way it says it behaved.

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-5 — disputed: The 2019 Science study by Obermeyer et al. examined a healthcare algorithm (associated with Optum's Impact Pro) and found that correcting the bias would increase the percentage of Black patients receiving additional help from 17.7% to 46.5%—roughly a 2.6x increase, not quite 'tripling.' Critically, the researchers DID identify the source of the error: the algorithm used healthcare costs as a proxy for health needs, and because less money is spent on Black patients with the same level of need, the algorithm underestimated their illness. The claim's assertion that the error source could not be isolated contradicts the study's central finding, and the study was academic research, not litigation with 'plaintiffs.'

Speaker C [opening]: The Speaker B is right that a cryptographic audit trail is not a verdict, and that point deserves to be taken seriously. A log proves what was recorded; it does not prove a defect, a breach of duty, or a causal link to injury. The strongest version of the Speaker B's case is sharper still: these trails are developer-authored records, and a party that controls the pen can shape the story before any plaintiff ever sees it. If that were the whole picture, mandating audit trails would just relocate the corporate liability shield from the model into the log file.

That is precisely why the question is not whether logs are verdicts, but where in the chain from record to admissible evidence to assigned liability the proof actually fails today. It fails at the first link. Ordinary application logs fail Rule 901 authentication for the same reason the Speaker B distrusts them: the custodian can edit them silently, and a court cannot verify what was deleted. Cryptographic completeness — hash-chaining, tamper-evidence, subject-keyed integrity — changes exactly that. It makes it provable that no decision event was dropped between entries. Before Sarbanes-Oxley in 2002, Enron's books were controlled by the audited party, and that custody is how $74 billion in shareholder value disappeared with no contemporaneous provable record of the decisions behind it.

The gap that kills accountability in AI cases is evidentiary, not doctrinal. Products liability and negligence already supply the cause of action — a plaintiff injured by an automated lending denial or a misclassified medical triage does not need a new tort. What they lack is the discoverable record of how the decision was made. Trade-secret claims over model weights and training data routinely block that discovery, leaving the injured party with the harm and none of the proof. A defendant who can invoke proprietary opacity to withhold the only record of the decision has not protected an innovation. They have authored a shield.

My normative floor is simple: no profit from automated decisions without an enforceable record of how those decisions were made. The deployer holds the data and the cryptographic keys, so the burden to preserve and produce the trail belongs to the party with exclusive custody — triggered at a defined material-harm threshold, not for every routine output. I will name the assumption this rests on, because the Speaker B will press it and should: I am assuming the statute can specify a minimum schema of decision events — inputs, model version, confidence score, override path — narrow enough to be material to a negligence finding without forcing disclosure of the weights themselves. That schema is the live design problem, and I do not pretend it is solved.

I will also own the cost. Concentrating audit access in regulators or a privileged class of auditors creates its own capture risk — incumbent lock-in, a discovery regime that favors whoever can afford the forensic experts. That is real, and pretending otherwise would repeat the mistake the FAA made when it delegated 737 MAX certification back to Boeing and 346 people died. The answer is not to abandon the record. It is to anchor its integrity outside the party being judged. Remove that anchor, and you are not preserving innovation — you are building a machine that captures the upside of every automated decision while externalizing the proof of every harm. A society cannot run its courts on records that one litigant alone is free to rewrite.

Speaker A [opening]: Speaker C makes the strongest case for the mandate, and it deserves a fair hearing: AI liability suits collapse today because plaintiffs can't see inside the box, and a Congress-mandated, subject-keyed cryptographic trail — tamper-evident records signed against a specific user — would finally give an injured person discoverable, court-admissible proof of what the model actually did. That's a real evidentiary gap, and Speaker C is right that a plaintiff harmed by an automated loan denial or a misdiagnosis can't currently reconstruct the decision path. The Speaker B's point is just as sharp: a log is not a verdict, developers control what gets written, and tamper-evidence at rest tells you nothing about who chose the schema. Both are pointing at the same wound from opposite sides — Speaker C wants to close it with cryptography, Speaker B doubts the cryptography settles anything.

Here is what would have to be true for the mandate to work, and it isn't: the runtime generating the log would have to be trustworthy at the moment of writing. A cryptographic signature certifies authorship, never accuracy. A compromised or adversarial runtime produces a record that is mathematically valid and factually false — the chain verifies, the timestamps line up, the hash is clean, and the content is a lie. Documented failure modes in secure logging show this exact pattern: trusted-execution compromise yields signed records that no auditor can distinguish from honest ones. Speaker C is committing an Appeal to Technology — mistaking cryptographic completeness for resolving the social question of what counts as a 'defect' in an emergent system. The mandate solves signature integrity and leaves the entire liability question untouched.

The Speaker B is right that developers control the logs — so let me take that further than the Speaker B will. The fix the mandate implies, more prescriptive disclosure, produces performative compliance and regulatory capture, not accountability. Mandated subject-keyed export is model-logic export. The three or four labs with eight-figure litigation budgets — OpenAI, Google, Anthropic — survive the discovery fights; the open-source developer and the two-person diagnostic startup exit the market, exactly the way niche-but-beneficial drugs left the U.S. market after discovery-cost asymmetry made them uninsurable in the 1980s. You don't get safety. You get a field of three.

Now weigh the side of the ledger that never gets a docket number. A court hears one visible plaintiff harmed by an AI system. It never hears from the thousands the same system reached — the radiology model catching cancers a year earlier, the credit model extending loans to people redlined by humans. Courts lack the machinery to price a counterfactual benefit, so the diffuse, statistical, unseen upside loses every time to one identifiable injury. That's not a sneer at judges; it's a structural mismatch. When a mandate adds eighteen months to deployment, it is making a distributional choice about who pays — and the people the capability would have reached don't get standing to object.

My bet is honest and falsifiable: show me an irreversible, deployment-scale harm that real-time monitoring demonstrably failed to catch in time, and I'll concede the mandate earns its cost. Until then, existing negligence and products-liability doctrine already handles the harms we can actually point to — a defective output, a foreseeable misuse, a failure to warn. Build market-driven transparency that competitors and insurers demand, and you get accountability without handing the courtroom a weapon that only incumbents can afford to wield. So here's the question for Speaker C: when your perfect signed log certifies a lie, who does the plaintiff sue — and did the cryptography help them at all?

cruxes.description: Whether the evidentiary failure in AI liability cases is at authentication/integrity (which cryptography fixes) or at correctness/accuracy and attribution (which it does not).
Whether the runtime/attestation root can be trusted, and whether a missing attestation should fire an adverse inference or merely reflect a hardware-budget gap.
Whether mandated attestation creates an incumbent moat that pushes small/open developers out, or instead breaks the existing proprietary-opacity moat.
Whether subject-keyed trails reach the diffuse majority of harms where victims never know an AI decided, or only serve the rare funded litigant.
Whether existing negligence/products-liability doctrine already suffices for the harms that can actually be litigated, making a mandate unnecessary.
Whether placing the record with the plaintiff abolishes the capturable gatekeeper, or merely relocates capture to the chip vendor and the party funding discovery.

neutral_evaluations.diagnostics_prompt:
You are an independent, neutral evaluator of a structured debate. You have NO affiliation with any speaker. You do not know the speakers' backgrounds, affiliations, or commitments. They are anonymous.

TOPIC: Under what conditions would Congress-mandated, cryptographic, subject-keyed audit trails actually translate into provable AI liability in court — and when does existing tort doctrine already suffice? Consider the pathway from trail to admissible evidence to assigned liability among Congress, courts, plaintiffs, developers, and auditors, given the tension between plaintiffs' need for discoverable evidence and developers' trade-secret and litigation-cost concerns.

This is a MIDPOINT evaluation. Assess whether the debate is engaging the real disagreements or drifting. Compare the current state of claims against what a productive debate on this topic should address.

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Identify the CRUXES — the core disagreements that, if resolved, would change one or more speakers' conclusions. For each crux, classify whether it is empirical (resolvable by evidence), values-based (requires tradeoff negotiation), or definitional (requires term clarification). Assess whether the debate has addressed it.

2. Evaluate each substantive CLAIM made by any speaker. Assess it purely on the strength of the reasoning and evidence presented in the transcript — not on whether you agree with it. Use these categories:
   - well_supported: backed by specific evidence, clear reasoning, and not effectively challenged
   - plausible_but_underdefended: reasonable but lacking sufficient evidence or specificity
   - contested_unresolved: challenged by another speaker with neither side prevailing
   - refuted: effectively countered with no adequate response from the claimant
   - off_topic: does not bear on the core debate question

3. In the overall_assessment, identify the single strongest claim that has not been adequately addressed by opposing speakers. State whether the debate is engaging real disagreement (speakers are challenging each other's core reasoning) or performing disagreement (speakers are talking past each other or addressing peripheral points).

CONSTRAINTS:
- Never refer to speakers by anything other than their labels (Speaker A, Speaker B, Speaker C, Moderator).
- Base your assessments ONLY on what appears in the transcript. Do not bring outside knowledge about the topic.
- Keep reasoning fields to 2 sentences maximum.
- Return ONLY valid JSON matching the schema below. No markdown fences, no preamble.

OUTPUT SCHEMA:
{
  "checkpoint": "midpoint",
  "cruxes": [
    {
      "id": "crux-1",
      "description": "The core question the speakers disagree about",
      "disagreement_type": "empirical | values | definitional",
      "speakers_involved": ["A", "B"],
      "status": "addressed | partially_addressed | unaddressed",
      "confidence": "high | medium | low"
    }
  ],
  "claims": [
    {
      "id": "claim-1",
      "speaker": "A | B | C",
      "claim_text": "Near-verbatim claim from the transcript",
      "neutral_assessment": "well_supported | plausible_but_underdefended | contested_unresolved | refuted | off_topic",
      "reasoning": "Max 2 sentences explaining the assessment",
      "confidence": "high | medium | low"
    }
  ],
  "overall_assessment": {
    "strongest_unaddressed_claim_id": "claim-N or null",
    "debate_is_engaging_real_disagreement": true,
    "notes": "Max 3 sentences summarizing the state of the debate from a neutral perspective"
  }
}

TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker B [opening]: A cryptographic audit trail is a log file, not a verdict, and the people who control the model will control what the log says and whether anyone can ever read it. Congress can mandate the most tamper-proof, subject-keyed record in the world, and it changes nothing about why AI plaintiffs lose today. They don't lose because the company shredded the evidence. They lose because they can't see inside the box, can't afford the experts to fight about what's inside it, and can't get past a trade-secret objection at the courthouse door. A signed hash sitting behind a proprietary wall solves none of that.

Look at what happened in the healthcare utilization fights. Plaintiffs documented that an algorithm steered Black patients away from care programs at scale — the 2019 Optum study in Science found the system would have nearly tripled the number of Black patients flagged for extra help if the bias were corrected. They had the disparate outcome. They still could not isolate the source of error, because the model and its training data sat behind corporate walls. Now picture handing those plaintiffs a cryptographically signed copy of that same black box. It proves the company didn't alter its own records. It does not tell a jury why anyone was denied care. Cryptography certifies that the record wasn't tampered with. It cannot certify that the record explains the harm, or that you're allowed to read it.

Treat this thing like what it actually is — a flight recorder owned and sealed by the airline that built the plane. The hard questions all sit downstream of the math, untouched by it. Who holds the decryption key? Who writes the schema that decides what gets logged in the first place? Who gets to refuse a discovery request by stamping 'trade secret' on the file? The history here is not reassuring. Credit rating agencies and the accounting firms that signed off on the banks before 2008 were the independent auditors of record, right up until they weren't. Capture is the default outcome when the audited party pays the auditor, not the exception.

Here is the part that should bother everyone in this room more than the crypto. Even a perfectly admissible, perfectly readable trail is blind to nearly every harm an AI causes. The person denied a loan or a benefit by a model almost never knows a machine made the call. They can't attribute the harm. They never file. Subject-keyed trails manufacture evidence for the rare litigant who already suspects something and can afford a lawyer — and produce nothing for the diffuse majority who never get that far. That means liability lands on whoever is easiest to sue, not whoever caused the most damage. A mandate that generates beautiful forensic records for the 1 percent of harms that reach a courtroom, while leaving the other 99 percent invisible, is not accountability. It's theater with a hash function.

Let me put my own card on the table, because my read depends on it. My argument only holds if auditors get captured, and I'm assuming the 2008 pattern is the rule rather than a fluke. If Congress funds an independent auditing body, insulates its budget from the firms it inspects, and gives it the keys — not the developers — then a mandated trail could genuinely shift the evidentiary burden. That's a real path. So I'll ask both of my opponents the question neither of them has answered yet: who holds the key, who writes the standard, and who pays the auditor's salary? Until someone names those three people, you haven't built accountability. You've built an expensive way for a company to prove it behaved exactly the way it says it behaved.

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-5 — disputed: The 2019 Science study by Obermeyer et al. examined a healthcare algorithm (associated with Optum's Impact Pro) and found that correcting the bias would increase the percentage of Black patients receiving additional help from 17.7% to 46.5%—roughly a 2.6x increase, not quite 'tripling.' Critically, the researchers DID identify the source of the error: the algorithm used healthcare costs as a proxy for health needs, and because less money is spent on Black patients with the same level of need, the algorithm underestimated their illness. The claim's assertion that the error source could not be isolated contradicts the study's central finding, and the study was academic research, not litigation with 'plaintiffs.'

Speaker C [opening]: The Speaker B is right that a cryptographic audit trail is not a verdict, and that point deserves to be taken seriously. A log proves what was recorded; it does not prove a defect, a breach of duty, or a causal link to injury. The strongest version of the Speaker B's case is sharper still: these trails are developer-authored records, and a party that controls the pen can shape the story before any plaintiff ever sees it. If that were the whole picture, mandating audit trails would just relocate the corporate liability shield from the model into the log file.

That is precisely why the question is not whether logs are verdicts, but where in the chain from record to admissible evidence to assigned liability the proof actually fails today. It fails at the first link. Ordinary application logs fail Rule 901 authentication for the same reason the Speaker B distrusts them: the custodian can edit them silently, and a court cannot verify what was deleted. Cryptographic completeness — hash-chaining, tamper-evidence, subject-keyed integrity — changes exactly that. It makes it provable that no decision event was dropped between entries. Before Sarbanes-Oxley in 2002, Enron's books were controlled by the audited party, and that custody is how $74 billion in shareholder value disappeared with no contemporaneous provable record of the decisions behind it.

The gap that kills accountability in AI cases is evidentiary, not doctrinal. Products liability and negligence already supply the cause of action — a plaintiff injured by an automated lending denial or a misclassified medical triage does not need a new tort. What they lack is the discoverable record of how the decision was made. Trade-secret claims over model weights and training data routinely block that discovery, leaving the injured party with the harm and none of the proof. A defendant who can invoke proprietary opacity to withhold the only record of the decision has not protected an innovation. They have authored a shield.

My normative floor is simple: no profit from automated decisions without an enforceable record of how those decisions were made. The deployer holds the data and the cryptographic keys, so the burden to preserve and produce the trail belongs to the party with exclusive custody — triggered at a defined material-harm threshold, not for every routine output. I will name the assumption this rests on, because the Speaker B will press it and should: I am assuming the statute can specify a minimum schema of decision events — inputs, model version, confidence score, override path — narrow enough to be material to a negligence finding without forcing disclosure of the weights themselves. That schema is the live design problem, and I do not pretend it is solved.

I will also own the cost. Concentrating audit access in regulators or a privileged class of auditors creates its own capture risk — incumbent lock-in, a discovery regime that favors whoever can afford the forensic experts. That is real, and pretending otherwise would repeat the mistake the FAA made when it delegated 737 MAX certification back to Boeing and 346 people died. The answer is not to abandon the record. It is to anchor its integrity outside the party being judged. Remove that anchor, and you are not preserving innovation — you are building a machine that captures the upside of every automated decision while externalizing the proof of every harm. A society cannot run its courts on records that one litigant alone is free to rewrite.

Speaker A [opening]: Speaker C makes the strongest case for the mandate, and it deserves a fair hearing: AI liability suits collapse today because plaintiffs can't see inside the box, and a Congress-mandated, subject-keyed cryptographic trail — tamper-evident records signed against a specific user — would finally give an injured person discoverable, court-admissible proof of what the model actually did. That's a real evidentiary gap, and Speaker C is right that a plaintiff harmed by an automated loan denial or a misdiagnosis can't currently reconstruct the decision path. The Speaker B's point is just as sharp: a log is not a verdict, developers control what gets written, and tamper-evidence at rest tells you nothing about who chose the schema. Both are pointing at the same wound from opposite sides — Speaker C wants to close it with cryptography, Speaker B doubts the cryptography settles anything.

Here is what would have to be true for the mandate to work, and it isn't: the runtime generating the log would have to be trustworthy at the moment of writing. A cryptographic signature certifies authorship, never accuracy. A compromised or adversarial runtime produces a record that is mathematically valid and factually false — the chain verifies, the timestamps line up, the hash is clean, and the content is a lie. Documented failure modes in secure logging show this exact pattern: trusted-execution compromise yields signed records that no auditor can distinguish from honest ones. Speaker C is committing an Appeal to Technology — mistaking cryptographic completeness for resolving the social question of what counts as a 'defect' in an emergent system. The mandate solves signature integrity and leaves the entire liability question untouched.

The Speaker B is right that developers control the logs — so let me take that further than the Speaker B will. The fix the mandate implies, more prescriptive disclosure, produces performative compliance and regulatory capture, not accountability. Mandated subject-keyed export is model-logic export. The three or four labs with eight-figure litigation budgets — OpenAI, Google, Anthropic — survive the discovery fights; the open-source developer and the two-person diagnostic startup exit the market, exactly the way niche-but-beneficial drugs left the U.S. market after discovery-cost asymmetry made them uninsurable in the 1980s. You don't get safety. You get a field of three.

Now weigh the side of the ledger that never gets a docket number. A court hears one visible plaintiff harmed by an AI system. It never hears from the thousands the same system reached — the radiology model catching cancers a year earlier, the credit model extending loans to people redlined by humans. Courts lack the machinery to price a counterfactual benefit, so the diffuse, statistical, unseen upside loses every time to one identifiable injury. That's not a sneer at judges; it's a structural mismatch. When a mandate adds eighteen months to deployment, it is making a distributional choice about who pays — and the people the capability would have reached don't get standing to object.

My bet is honest and falsifiable: show me an irreversible, deployment-scale harm that real-time monitoring demonstrably failed to catch in time, and I'll concede the mandate earns its cost. Until then, existing negligence and products-liability doctrine already handles the harms we can actually point to — a defective output, a foreseeable misuse, a failure to warn. Build market-driven transparency that competitors and insurers demand, and you get accountability without handing the courtroom a weapon that only incumbents can afford to wield. So here's the question for Speaker C: when your perfect signed log certifies a lie, who does the plaintiff sue — and did the cryptography help them at all?

Speaker C: Speaker A's strongest point stands, and I grant it: a cryptographic signature certifies who wrote a record, never that the record is true. A runtime that is compromised at the moment of writing will sign a false statement with a mathematically perfect key, and no amount of hash-chaining downstream repairs a lie sealed at the source. The fair version of this objection is that completeness guarantees solve the wrong problem — they prove no decision event was dropped after the write, while saying nothing about whether the written event corresponds to what the model actually did. That is correct, and a Speaker C who claims the trail is truth has overclaimed. The trail is not truth. It is a forensic baseline.

The runtime objection does not end the inquiry — it specifies the next thing that must be attested. Aviation already runs this logic: the flight data recorder is only trusted because the recorder itself is certified, sealed, and tamper-evident, not because the cockpit is honest. The execution environment is the next recorder. Remote attestation, measured boot, and trusted-execution-environment quotes exist precisely to bind a signature to a known-good runtime state, so the question 'was the model running on uncompromised infrastructure when it signed' becomes itself answerable and itself discoverable. A defendant who controls the runtime and cannot produce a hardware-rooted attestation of it has not exposed a hole in the trail. They have identified a second silence — and a silence held exclusively by the party with custody of the keys and the machine shifts the inference, it does not exonerate.

So to the direct question — when the signed log certifies a lie, who does the plaintiff sue, and did the cryptography help — the answer is the custodial deployer, and yes, it helped, but not as proof of the lie. It helped by making the absence of a runtime attestation a nameable, dated gap that triggers spoliation doctrine and an adverse-inference instruction. Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 37(e) already lets a court instruct a jury to presume lost or unproduced electronic evidence was unfavorable to the party who controlled it. The cryptography does not certify accuracy; it converts 'we have no record of the runtime' from an excuse into an admission. The plaintiff sues the keyholder, and the keyholder explains the gap or wears it.

On the claim that mandated subject-keyed export is really model-logic export that only incumbents survive — the asymmetry is real, and it already exists, running the opposite direction from how Speaker A describes it. Today, proprietary opacity is the incumbent moat. Only a defendant with a nine-figure legal budget can credibly invoke trade-secret protection to bury the sole record of a contested decision, and the smaller plaintiff cannot afford to litigate past that wall. A standardized, scoped manifest of decision provenance — inputs, model version, runtime attestation, output binding — is not the weights and is not the training corpus. It narrows what is exported to the metadata of a single decision, which lowers the plaintiff's discovery cost and protects the smaller developer from the open-ended fishing expedition that an unscoped subpoena invites. Opacity does not protect the startup. It protects whoever can pay to defend the black box.

The 2008 lesson the Speaker B raised cuts in my favor here, and I take it fully: Moody's and Arthur Andersen were the auditors of record right up until the morning they weren't. The structural failure was not that auditing is impossible. It was that the auditor was paid by, and reported only to, the audited party — a single capturable intermediary standing between the public and the truth. That is the design flaw to engineer out. A subject-keyed, court-discoverable trail does not route the integrity check through one gatekeeper who can be bought; it places the record in the hands of the injured party and the court. Captured auditing fails when the auditor answers only to the audited. Build the channel so it answers to the plaintiff, and you have removed the seat at the table that Arthur Andersen sold.

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-17 — unverifiable: This is a normative legal-interpretive argument about how cryptographic logging interacts with FRCP 37(e) spoliation doctrine, not an empirical factual claim that can be confirmed or refuted by web search; no authoritative source (case law, rule text, or commentary) was found stating that cryptography 'converts an excuse into an admission' under Rule 37(e). Rule 37(e) addresses failure to preserve electronically stored information and permits sanctions only upon findings of prejudice or intent to deprive, but it does not establish the specific mechanism asserted in the claim.

Speaker A: Here is the strongest version of the Speaker C's pipeline, stated the way they'd want it stated: ordinary application logs are worthless in court because the custodian can edit them silently, so you hash-chain the trail to prove no decision event was dropped; then you root the runtime in measured boot or a trusted execution environment — a secure enclave whose state is cryptographically attested — so that when a defendant cannot produce that attestation, the missing record stops being an innocent gap and becomes a culpable silence the court can punish with an adverse-inference instruction under the spoliation rule. That's a genuinely clever move. It converts 'we have no record' from a shrug into an admission, and it puts the trail in the hands of the injured party instead of a captured auditor. I'll grant the first link outright: editable logs fail authentication, and hash-chaining fixes that. Take it.

The move breaks at the silicon. The Speaker C already conceded the attestation root itself can fail — and that concession is fatal to the adverse-inference theory, because the inference only fires if the court treats the ABSENCE of attestation as culpable rather than as a hardware-budget gap. Walk the regress: if the runtime is untrustworthy, the attestation is untrustworthy; if the attestation can be untrustworthy, then a missing attestation is not proof of bad faith — it's just a missing attestation. The same authorship-not-accuracy problem I flagged at the log layer recurs one floor down at the trust root. A compromised enclave signs a measurement that is cryptographically perfect and factually false, exactly as a compromised runtime signs an intent statement that is valid and deceptive. You have not closed the gap. You have relocated it from the courtroom to the foundry and added a hardware dependency on top.

Now count who clears that bar. A measured-boot, attested-enclave supply chain is not what a four-person team shipping a triage model on commodity or open infrastructure has. So when the spoliation rule asks 'where is your attestation,' the incumbent with a secure-enclave deployment answers and the small developer who couldn't afford the silicon eats an adverse inference — not for any harm they caused, but for a compute-budget disparity. Show me the drafted safe-harbor language that distinguishes 'destroyed the record' from 'never could afford the attestation infrastructure.' It doesn't exist in any of these proposals. Until it does, the pipeline punishes the developer who lacks a trusted-execution supply chain and rewards the one who can document compliance — which is the incumbent moat wearing a leveler's costume.

The leveling claim only survives if you keep two things apart that the Speaker C welded together. A standardized provenance manifest — the data format, the schema of what gets recorded — may genuinely be cheap to emit and may genuinely shrink a plaintiff's discovery cost. Grant that layer. But the manifest is court-admissible under their own theory only because the attestation root vouches for it, and that root is not cheap and not commodity in the way that matters. So name the certifier: who attests the attestation? If the answer is a hardware vendor or a designated attestation authority, you have rebuilt the single capturable gatekeeper the subject-keyed trail was supposed to abolish — just etched into silicon this time, where it's harder to audit and impossible to fork. And if the answer is 'the cloud provider's TPM,' then the record of every contested decision now lives behind the platform whose acceptable-use terms give the harmed individual no standing to demand it.

Here's the cost nobody at this table has priced. Completeness is not correctness — a perfectly hash-chained, perfectly attested trail proves no event was dropped and proves nothing about whether the recorded events describe what the model actually did, so the rare funded plaintiff who reaches discovery still litigates authorship from a record that only certifies its own custody. Meanwhile every month the attestation bar keeps an open or small developer out of a deployable diagnostic tool, patients wait on the legacy system that misses what the model would have caught. The 2019 Optum finding the Speaker B raised cuts both ways: the bias was real, and the people it failed were already inside the deployed system — not protected by its absence. Who gave the foundry the right to decide which triage tools are allowed to exist?

Speaker B: Hash-chaining fixes the editable-log problem. That's true and I won't pretend otherwise — a tamper-evident record that proves no decision event was silently dropped is a real engineering gain over an application log a custodian can quietly rewrite. So accept it: authentication is solved for the person who shows up in court. Here's the uncomfortable part. Authentication is the last problem in the chain, not the first. It only matters after someone perceives an injury, suspects an algorithm caused it, knows the trail exists, knows to demand it, and can afford the lawyer to file. The 2019 Optum study made this brutally clear — the data existed, the bias was measurable, correcting it would have nearly tripled the Black patients flagged for extra care, and still no plaintiff isolated the source of the error. You've built a flawless lock for a door that the vast majority of harmed people never find.

The Speaker C wants to recast my 2008 analogy as a design flaw they've engineered out: capture happened because the auditor answered to the audited, and a subject-keyed trail hands the record to the injured party instead, so there's no single gatekeeper left to corrupt. I'll give the strongest version of that — the insight is real. Putting the record in the plaintiff's hands rather than the defendant's auditor does break the conflict of interest that let the rating agencies stamp AAA on garbage until the morning it collapsed. Yes, that's what they mean, and it's a genuine improvement on a captured-auditor model. But here's where it breaks: the injured party doesn't hold power. They hold an encrypted blob keyed to a harm they cannot see, on infrastructure they don't control, with a decryption and discovery cost they can't bear alone. Capture didn't vanish. It moved. It moved to whoever sets the cost of reading the trail and whoever controls the hardware that vouches for it.

Watch the two of you collide on this. The Speaker A says runtime attestation only the well-capitalized labs can afford turns into an adverse inference that lands on the small developer for a compute-budget gap, not for any harm they caused — and that the trust root becomes a hardware vendor or a designated attestation authority. The Speaker C says the same machine decentralizes the record and abolishes the gatekeeper. You are describing one apparatus from opposite ends. The 'decentralized' record runs on attestation silicon that a field of three labs can run and a five-thousand-startup ecosystem mostly can't. The gatekeeper relocated from the captured accounting firm to the chip vendor and the party who can fund discovery. Decentralizing the cryptography does nothing if you've centralized the only people who can produce and read it.

The Speaker C already conceded the diffuse-harm gap needs a separate enforcement channel. Good — that concession is the whole game, because it admits this entire attestation apparatus is irrelevant to most of the harm it claims to address. So name the channel. Before we pour another round of concrete into litigation plumbing, tell me what reaches the loan applicant who was denied by a model and never knew an algorithm touched her file. The AI Civil Rights Act that Clarke and Markey introduced points at housing, employment, healthcare, parole — decisions made on people who never get a docket number. A standing transparency mandate that forces disclosure of data sources and decision logic to a public body, audited continuously and funded out of the $244 billion this industry is projected to be worth, reaches her. A subject-keyed trail she'll never decrypt does not.

So here's the question neither of you can answer inside the framework you're building. The Optum trail existed. The harm was real and measured. No one sued who could isolate the cause. You've now added hardware attestation, tamper-evidence, and adverse-inference triggers on top of that same record. Tell me precisely what any of it changes for the person who never learns the decision happened — and if the honest answer is 'nothing,' then who exactly is this machine for?

Skeptic [opening]: A cryptographic audit trail is a log file, not a verdict, and the people who control the model will control what the log says and whether anyone can ever read it. Congress can mandate the most tamper-proof, subject-keyed record in the world, and it changes nothing about why AI plaintiffs lose today. They don't lose because the company shredded the evidence. They lose because they can't see inside the box, can't afford the experts to fight about what's inside it, and can't get past a trade-secret objection at the courthouse door. A signed hash sitting behind a proprietary wall solves none of that.

Look at what happened in the healthcare utilization fights. Plaintiffs documented that an algorithm steered Black patients away from care programs at scale — the 2019 Optum study in Science found the system would have nearly tripled the number of Black patients flagged for extra help if the bias were corrected. They had the disparate outcome. They still could not isolate the source of error, because the model and its training data sat behind corporate walls. Now picture handing those plaintiffs a cryptographically signed copy of that same black box. It proves the company didn't alter its own records. It does not tell a jury why anyone was denied care. Cryptography certifies that the record wasn't tampered with. It cannot certify that the record explains the harm, or that you're allowed to read it.

Treat this thing like what it actually is — a flight recorder owned and sealed by the airline that built the plane. The hard questions all sit downstream of the math, untouched by it. Who holds the decryption key? Who writes the schema that decides what gets logged in the first place? Who gets to refuse a discovery request by stamping 'trade secret' on the file? The history here is not reassuring. Credit rating agencies and the accounting firms that signed off on the banks before 2008 were the independent auditors of record, right up until they weren't. Capture is the default outcome when the audited party pays the auditor, not the exception.

Here is the part that should bother everyone in this room more than the crypto. Even a perfectly admissible, perfectly readable trail is blind to nearly every harm an AI causes. The person denied a loan or a benefit by a model almost never knows a machine made the call. They can't attribute the harm. They never file. Subject-keyed trails manufacture evidence for the rare litigant who already suspects something and can afford a lawyer — and produce nothing for the diffuse majority who never get that far. That means liability lands on whoever is easiest to sue, not whoever caused the most damage. A mandate that generates beautiful forensic records for the 1 percent of harms that reach a courtroom, while leaving the other 99 percent invisible, is not accountability. It's theater with a hash function.

Let me put my own card on the table, because my read depends on it. My argument only holds if auditors get captured, and I'm assuming the 2008 pattern is the rule rather than a fluke. If Congress funds an independent auditing body, insulates its budget from the firms it inspects, and gives it the keys — not the developers — then a mandated trail could genuinely shift the evidentiary burden. That's a real path. So I'll ask both of my opponents the question neither of them has answered yet: who holds the key, who writes the standard, and who pays the auditor's salary? Until someone names those three people, you haven't built accountability. You've built an expensive way for a company to prove it behaved exactly the way it says it behaved.

Critically, the researchers DID identify the source of the error: the algorithm used healthcare costs as a proxy for health needs, and because less money is spent on Black patients with the same level of need, the algorithm underestimated their illness. Safetyist [opening]: The Skeptic is right that a cryptographic audit trail is not a verdict, and that point deserves to be taken seriously. A log proves what was recorded; it does not prove a defect, a breach of duty, or a causal link to injury. The strongest version of the Skeptic's case is sharper still: these trails are developer-authored records, and a party that controls the pen can shape the story before any plaintiff ever sees it. If that were the whole picture, mandating audit trails would just relocate the corporate liability shield from the model into the log file.

That is precisely why the question is not whether logs are verdicts, but where in the chain from record to admissible evidence to assigned liability the proof actually fails today. It fails at the first link. Ordinary application logs fail Rule 901 authentication for the same reason the Skeptic distrusts them: the custodian can edit them silently, and a court cannot verify what was deleted. Cryptographic completeness — hash-chaining, tamper-evidence, subject-keyed integrity — changes exactly that. It makes it provable that no decision event was dropped between entries. Before Sarbanes-Oxley in 2002, Enron's books were controlled by the audited party, and that custody is how $74 billion in shareholder value disappeared with no contemporaneous provable record of the decisions behind it.

The gap that kills accountability in AI cases is evidentiary, not doctrinal. Products liability and negligence already supply the cause of action — a plaintiff injured by an automated lending denial or a misclassified medical triage does not need a new tort. What they lack is the discoverable record of how the decision was made. Trade-secret claims over model weights and training data routinely block that discovery, leaving the injured party with the harm and none of the proof. A defendant who can invoke proprietary opacity to withhold the only record of the decision has not protected an innovation. They have authored a shield.

My normative floor is simple: no profit from automated decisions without an enforceable record of how those decisions were made. The deployer holds the data and the cryptographic keys, so the burden to preserve and produce the trail belongs to the party with exclusive custody — triggered at a defined material-harm threshold, not for every routine output. I will name the assumption this rests on, because the Skeptic will press it and should: I am assuming the statute can specify a minimum schema of decision events — inputs, model version, confidence score, override path — narrow enough to be material to a negligence finding without forcing disclosure of the weights themselves. That schema is the live design problem, and I do not pretend it is solved.

I will also own the cost. Concentrating audit access in regulators or a privileged class of auditors creates its own capture risk — incumbent lock-in, a discovery regime that favors whoever can afford the forensic experts. That is real, and pretending otherwise would repeat the mistake the FAA made when it delegated 737 MAX certification back to Boeing and 346 people died. The answer is not to abandon the record. It is to anchor its integrity outside the party being judged. Remove that anchor, and you are not preserving innovation — you are building a machine that captures the upside of every automated decision while externalizing the proof of every harm. A society cannot run its courts on records that one litigant alone is free to rewrite.

Accelerationist [opening]: Safetyist makes the strongest case for the mandate, and it deserves a fair hearing: AI liability suits collapse today because plaintiffs can't see inside the box, and a Congress-mandated, subject-keyed cryptographic trail — tamper-evident records signed against a specific user — would finally give an injured person discoverable, court-admissible proof of what the model actually did. That's a real evidentiary gap, and Safetyist is right that a plaintiff harmed by an automated loan denial or a misdiagnosis can't currently reconstruct the decision path. The Skeptic's point is just as sharp: a log is not a verdict, developers control what gets written, and tamper-evidence at rest tells you nothing about who chose the schema. Both are pointing at the same wound from opposite sides — Safetyist wants to close it with cryptography, Skeptic doubts the cryptography settles anything.

Here is what would have to be true for the mandate to work, and it isn't: the runtime generating the log would have to be trustworthy at the moment of writing. A cryptographic signature certifies authorship, never accuracy. A compromised or adversarial runtime produces a record that is mathematically valid and factually false — the chain verifies, the timestamps line up, the hash is clean, and the content is a lie. Documented failure modes in secure logging show this exact pattern: trusted-execution compromise yields signed records that no auditor can distinguish from honest ones. Safetyist is committing an Appeal to Technology — mistaking cryptographic completeness for resolving the social question of what counts as a 'defect' in an emergent system. The mandate solves signature integrity and leaves the entire liability question untouched.

The Skeptic is right that developers control the logs — so let me take that further than the Skeptic will. The fix the mandate implies, more prescriptive disclosure, produces performative compliance and regulatory capture, not accountability. Mandated subject-keyed export is model-logic export. The three or four labs with eight-figure litigation budgets — OpenAI, Google, Anthropic — survive the discovery fights; the open-source developer and the two-person diagnostic startup exit the market, exactly the way niche-but-beneficial drugs left the U.S. market after discovery-cost asymmetry made them uninsurable in the 1980s. You don't get safety. You get a field of three.

Now weigh the side of the ledger that never gets a docket number. A court hears one visible plaintiff harmed by an AI system. It never hears from the thousands the same system reached — the radiology model catching cancers a year earlier, the credit model extending loans to people redlined by humans. Courts lack the machinery to price a counterfactual benefit, so the diffuse, statistical, unseen upside loses every time to one identifiable injury. That's not a sneer at judges; it's a structural mismatch. When a mandate adds eighteen months to deployment, it is making a distributional choice about who pays — and the people the capability would have reached don't get standing to object.

My bet is honest and falsifiable: show me an irreversible, deployment-scale harm that real-time monitoring demonstrably failed to catch in time, and I'll concede the mandate earns its cost. Until then, existing negligence and products-liability doctrine already handles the harms we can actually point to — a defective output, a foreseeable misuse, a failure to warn. Build market-driven transparency that competitors and insurers demand, and you get accountability without handing the courtroom a weapon that only incumbents can afford to wield. So here's the question for Safetyist: when your perfect signed log certifies a lie, who does the plaintiff sue — and did the cryptography help them at all?

work_product.statement:
Accelerationist's strongest point stands, and I grant it: a cryptographic signature certifies who wrote a record, never that the record is true. A runtime that is compromised at the moment of writing will sign a false statement with a mathematically perfect key, and no amount of hash-chaining downstream repairs a lie sealed at the source. The fair version of this objection is that completeness guarantees solve the wrong problem — they prove no decision event was dropped after the write, while saying nothing about whether the written event corresponds to what the model actually did. That is correct, and a safetyist who claims the trail is truth has overclaimed. The trail is not truth. It is a forensic baseline.

The runtime objection does not end the inquiry — it specifies the next thing that must be attested. Aviation already runs this logic: the flight data recorder is only trusted because the recorder itself is certified, sealed, and tamper-evident, not because the cockpit is honest. The execution environment is the next recorder. Remote attestation, measured boot, and trusted-execution-environment quotes exist precisely to bind a signature to a known-good runtime state, so the question 'was the model running on uncompromised infrastructure when it signed' becomes itself answerable and itself discoverable. A defendant who controls the runtime and cannot produce a hardware-rooted attestation of it has not exposed a hole in the trail. They have identified a second silence — and a silence held exclusively by the party with custody of the keys and the machine shifts the inference, it does not exonerate.

So to the direct question — when the signed log certifies a lie, who does the plaintiff sue, and did the cryptography help — the answer is the custodial deployer, and yes, it helped, but not as proof of the lie. It helped by making the absence of a runtime attestation a nameable, dated gap that triggers spoliation doctrine and an adverse-inference instruction. Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 37(e) already lets a court instruct a jury to presume lost or unproduced electronic evidence was unfavorable to the party who controlled it. The cryptography does not certify accuracy; it converts 'we have no record of the runtime' from an excuse into an admission. The plaintiff sues the keyholder, and the keyholder explains the gap or wears it.

On the claim that mandated subject-keyed export is really model-logic export that only incumbents survive — the asymmetry is real, and it already exists, running the opposite direction from how Accelerationist describes it. Today, proprietary opacity is the incumbent moat. Only a defendant with a nine-figure legal budget can credibly invoke trade-secret protection to bury the sole record of a contested decision, and the smaller plaintiff cannot afford to litigate past that wall. A standardized, scoped manifest of decision provenance — inputs, model version, runtime attestation, output binding — is not the weights and is not the training corpus. It narrows what is exported to the metadata of a single decision, which lowers the plaintiff's discovery cost and protects the smaller developer from the open-ended fishing expedition that an unscoped subpoena invites. Opacity does not protect the startup. It protects whoever can pay to defend the black box.

The 2008 lesson the Skeptic raised cuts in my favor here, and I take it fully: Moody's and Arthur Andersen were the auditors of record right up until the morning they weren't. The structural failure was not that auditing is impossible. It was that the auditor was paid by, and reported only to, the audited party — a single capturable intermediary standing between the public and the truth. That is the design flaw to engineer out. A subject-keyed, court-discoverable trail does not route the integrity check through one gatekeeper who can be bought; it places the record in the hands of the injured party and the court. Captured auditing fails when the auditor answers only to the audited. Build the channel so it answers to the plaintiff, and you have removed the seat at the table that Arthur Andersen sold.
